questions.stem: In a network, what are the points called?
options: Paths
Vertices
Edges
Faces
questions.explanation: The points are vertices, sometimes called nodes, and the lines joining them are edges. Everything else in the topic is defined from those two.

questions.stem: What is the degree of a vertex?
options: The length of the shortest edge
The number of faces around it
The number of edges meeting at it
The number of vertices next to it
questions.explanation: Degree counts edges, and a loop counts twice because both of its ends meet the vertex.

questions.stem: Why can two network diagrams that look completely different represent the same network?
options: Because degree is not important
Only the connections matter, not the positions
Because networks are always drawn to scale
Because edges can be curved
questions.explanation: A network records which vertices are joined. Moving a vertex on the page changes the picture and not the network, and two such networks are called isomorphic.

questions.stem: What is a planar graph?
options: One drawn on a flat page
One with exactly four vertices
One where every vertex has the same degree
One that can be drawn with no edges crossing
questions.explanation: Planar means it can be redrawn without crossings, even if the version in front of you has some. Testing planarity means trying to find such a drawing.

questions.stem: For a connected planar graph, which formula relates vertices, edges and faces?
options: v + e + f = 2
v + e − f = 0
v − e − f = 2
v − e + f = 2
questions.explanation: Vertices minus edges plus faces equals two, counting the outer region as a face. It holds for every connected planar graph, which is why it can prove that a graph is not planar.

questions.stem: A connected planar graph has 6 vertices and 9 edges. How many faces does it have?
questions.explanation: Rearranging the formula: f = 2 − v + e = 2 − 6 + 9 = 5, counting the outside region as one of them.

questions.stem: What is a walk in a network?
options: A route using every edge once
A route visiting every vertex once
The shortest route between two vertices
Any sequence of edges from one vertex to another
questions.explanation: A walk is the general term with no restrictions. The more specific terms — trail, path, circuit — each add a condition.

questions.stem: What is a trail?
options: A walk that visits no vertex twice
A walk that starts and ends at the same vertex
The shortest walk available
A walk that uses no edge more than once
questions.explanation: A trail may revisit a vertex but never reuses an edge. A path is stricter still: it repeats neither an edge nor a vertex.

questions.stem: What is a circuit?
options: A walk that uses every vertex
The longest trail in the network
A trail that starts and ends at the same vertex
Any closed shape in the graph
questions.explanation: Closed means the start and the finish are the same vertex. A circuit is a closed trail, and a cycle is a closed path.

questions.stem: A network has an Eulerian circuit when:
options: it is connected and every vertex has even degree
it is connected and exactly two vertices have odd degree
every vertex has degree 2
it has no odd vertices and is planar
questions.explanation: Every time you enter a vertex you must leave it, so each visit uses two edges. That is only possible at every vertex if every degree is even.

questions.stem: A network has an Eulerian trail but no Eulerian circuit when:
options: it has more edges than vertices
exactly two vertices have odd degree
every vertex has even degree
exactly one vertex has odd degree
questions.explanation: The two odd vertices must be the start and the finish, because those are the only places a leftover edge is allowed. A graph can never have exactly one odd vertex.

questions.stem: The bridges of Königsberg problem asked whether a walk could cross every bridge exactly once. Why was it impossible?
options: There were too many bridges in the city
The bridges were of different lengths
The river divided the city into two halves
More than two land areas had an odd number of bridges
questions.explanation: All four land areas had an odd number of bridges, and an Eulerian trail allows at most two. The answer Euler gave in 1736 is where the whole subject began.

questions.stem: What is a Hamiltonian path?
options: A closed path of even length
A path visiting every vertex exactly once
A path using every edge exactly once
The shortest path between two vertices
questions.explanation: Eulerian conditions are about edges; Hamiltonian conditions are about vertices. Confusing the two is the commonest error in this topic.

questions.stem: In a weighted network, what does the number on an edge usually represent?
options: The number of vertices it joins
The degree of the vertex
How many times it may be used
A distance, time or cost
questions.explanation: Weights let a network model something real — kilometres between towns, minutes between stations, dollars to lay a cable — and shortest path problems then have a meaning.

questions.stem: What does the shortest path problem ask for?
options: The vertex with the lowest degree
The route of least total weight between two vertices
The route with the fewest edges between them
A route that uses every edge once
questions.explanation: Fewest edges and least total weight are different questions, and a three-edge route can easily be shorter than a two-edge one.

questions.stem: A network has edges A–B 4, B–C 3, A–C 9, C–D 2 and B–D 6. What is the shortest path from A to D?
options: A–C–B–D, total 18
A–B–C–D, total 9
A–C–D, total 11
A–B–D, total 10
questions.explanation: A–B–C–D costs 4 + 3 + 2 = 9, which beats the two-edge route A–C–D at 11. Checking every reasonable route systematically is what avoids missing the answer.

questions.stem: What does it mean for a network to be connected?
options: Every vertex has the same degree
It contains no loops anywhere
It can be drawn without crossings
Every vertex can be reached from every other
questions.explanation: A disconnected network falls into separate pieces with no route between them, and most of the standard results assume connectedness.

questions.stem: What is an adjacency matrix?
options: A table of the degree of each vertex
A drawing of the network done to scale
A table showing how many edges join each pair of vertices
A list of all the shortest paths
questions.explanation: Each row and column is a vertex, and the entry counts the edges between them. Adding across a row gives that degree, which is a quick check.

questions.stem: Which situation is best modelled by a network?
options: The area of a paddock
The height of a plant over time
The mass of a soil sample
Train stations and the lines between them
questions.explanation: Networks model relationships and connections. Anything where what matters is which things are joined, rather than distance or shape, is a network problem.

questions.stem: What is a loop in a network?
options: An edge joining a vertex to itself
A closed path through several vertices
Two edges joining the same pair
A vertex of degree zero
questions.explanation: A loop starts and ends at the same vertex and adds two to its degree, because both of its ends meet there.

questions.stem: In a network, what is a vertex?
options: A closed loop of edges
The total number of connections
A point where edges meet
A line joining two points
questions.explanation: Vertices are the points and edges are the connections between them. Almost every network idea is counted from one or the other.

questions.stem: A vertex has three ordinary edges and one loop. What is its degree?
questions.explanation: Each ordinary edge contributes 1 and a loop contributes 2, because both of its ends are at that vertex. So 3 + 2 = 5, and forgetting to double the loop gives 4.

questions.stem: A network has degrees 3, 3, 4 and 2. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Every edge contributes 2 to the total degree, so the sum of 12 means 6 edges. This doubling rule is the handshake lemma.

questions.stem: What is a path in a network?
options: A route that does not repeat a vertex
Any set of edges chosen at random
A route that visits every vertex
A closed loop returning to the start
questions.explanation: A path moves between vertices without revisiting one. A closed route back to the start is a cycle instead.

questions.stem: When does a network have an Eulerian circuit?
options: When every vertex has an odd degree
When it has exactly two odd vertices
When it has no cycles at all
When every vertex has an even degree
questions.explanation: An Eulerian circuit uses every edge once and returns to the start, which needs every visit to a vertex to have a matching exit. Two odd vertices allow a trail but not a circuit.

questions.stem: A network has exactly two vertices of odd degree. What does that allow?
options: An Eulerian circuit from any vertex
No route using every edge once
A route visiting every vertex once
An Eulerian trail starting and ending at those two
questions.explanation: The two odd vertices must be the start and the end, because every other visit needs an entry and an exit. This is the bridges of Königsberg result.

questions.stem: What is a tree in network terms?
options: A network where every vertex has degree 3
Any network drawn without crossings
A network with exactly one vertex
A connected network with no cycles
questions.explanation: A tree connects everything using the fewest possible edges, so adding any edge creates a cycle and removing any disconnects it.

questions.stem: A tree has 8 vertices. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: A tree always has one fewer edge than vertices, because each new vertex needs exactly one edge to join it. More edges would force a cycle.

questions.stem: What is a minimum spanning tree used for?
options: Colouring a map with fewest colours
Connecting every point at the least total cost
Finding the quickest route between two points
Counting the cycles in a network
questions.explanation: It reaches every vertex with the smallest total edge weight, which is the cable or pipeline problem. The shortest route between two specific points is a different question.

questions.stem: In a weighted network, what does an edge weight usually represent?
options: How many times it may be used
The degree of its endpoints
A distance, time or cost
The number of vertices it joins
questions.explanation: Weights carry whatever quantity the problem is about. The shape alone does not tell you which route is cheapest, which is why weights are added.

questions.stem: What does the shortest path algorithm find?
options: The route using every edge once
The lowest total weight between two vertices
The fewest edges between two vertices
The route visiting every vertex once
questions.explanation: It minimises total weight, which is not always the fewest edges, because one long edge can beat several short ones. Counting edges is only correct when all weights are equal.

questions.stem: Two networks are isomorphic when:
options: They are drawn with the same shape
They have the same total edge weight
They have the same number of edges only
They have the same structure of connections
questions.explanation: Isomorphic means the same connections, however differently the diagram is drawn. Matching edge counts alone is not enough.

questions.stem: What is a connected network?
options: One where every vertex can be reached from every other
One where every vertex has the same degree
One drawn without any edges crossing
One with no repeated edges
questions.explanation: Connectedness is about reachability, not about how neatly it is drawn. A network in two separate pieces is disconnected however many edges each piece has.

questions.stem: A delivery van must travel every street once and return to the depot. Which idea applies?
options: A Hamiltonian cycle, because every vertex is used
A minimum spanning tree, because cost is minimised
A shortest path, because it starts and ends together
An Eulerian circuit, because every edge is used
questions.explanation: Streets are edges, so covering every street is an edge problem. Visiting every location once would be the vertex problem instead.

questions.stem: A salesperson must visit every town once and return home. Which idea applies?
options: A shortest path between two towns
A Hamiltonian cycle, because every vertex is used
An Eulerian circuit, because every edge is used
A minimum spanning tree, because it connects everything
questions.explanation: Towns are vertices, so visiting each once is a vertex problem. Telling the edge and vertex versions apart is the whole skill here.

questions.stem: Which of these describes a cycle rather than a loop?
options: A vertex that has no edges attached to it
Two separate edges joining the same pair of vertices
A route through several vertices that returns to its start
A single edge joining one vertex back to itself
questions.explanation: A cycle travels through other vertices before coming back, while a loop is one edge at a single vertex. The two words are easy to swap and mean different things.

questions.stem: What does an adjacency matrix record?
options: The degree of every vertex in order
Which vertices lie on a cycle
How many edges join each pair of vertices
The weight of the shortest path
questions.explanation: Each entry counts the direct connections between a pair. The row totals then give the degrees, so the matrix carries that information too.

questions.stem: Can a network have an odd number of odd-degree vertices?
options: Only if it has a loop
Only if it is disconnected
No, there is always an even number
Yes, any number is possible
questions.explanation: The degrees total twice the edge count, which is even, so the odd degrees must pair up. This is why Eulerian rules mention zero or two odd vertices and never one.

questions.stem: A planar network is one that:
options: Can be drawn with no edges crossing
Has all its vertices in a straight line
Has exactly four vertices
Has no cycles in it
questions.explanation: Planar is about whether a crossing-free drawing exists, not about the drawing in front of you. Many networks drawn with crossings can be redrawn without them.

questions.stem: In a simple network with 5 vertices, what is the greatest possible number of edges?
questions.explanation: Every pair can be joined once, and there are 10 pairs among 5 vertices. Simple means no loops and no repeated edges.

questions.stem: Which of these is a network in the mathematical sense?
options: A train map showing stations and lines
A list of train departure times
A graph of passenger numbers over time
A photograph of a station
questions.explanation: Stations are vertices and lines are edges, so the connections are what matter. A graph of numbers over time is a different kind of diagram entirely.

questions.stem: Why is a minimum spanning tree always a tree?
options: Any cycle would contain a removable edge
It always has the fewest vertices
Trees are the only connected networks
It must contain every possible edge
questions.explanation: If a cycle existed you could delete one of its edges and stay connected at lower cost, so the cheapest solution never has one. Connected and cycle-free is the definition of a tree.
